note: The shared source list. Each source is written up once here and cited by id from entries. 'checked' says who opened it, when, which copy they read and in what language. Claude may mark a source checked only after reading the passage in a copy anyone can open (source standards, decided by Marc on 4 Nov 2026); Marc spot-checks a sample.

sources.reference: Annales Bertiniani (Annals of St-Bertin), the part for 862–882 written by Hincmar, archbishop of Reims. Latin edition: G. sources.distance_note: Hincmar's part of the annals covers 862 to 882 and dates from the second half of the 9th century (Mapping Medieval Peoples database, text record 581).

sources.reference: Annales Fuldenses (Annals of Fulda), with the Bavarian continuations for 882–901. Latin edition: F. Kurze (ed.), Annales Fuldenses sive Annales regni Francorum orientalis, Scriptores rerum Germanicarum in usum scholarum (Hanover, 1891). The years 892–896 are on pp. 121–130 (Regensburg continuation) and 900–901 on pp. 134–135 (Altaich continuation).
sources.distance_note: Kurze's preface says the first Bavarian continuation was added at Regensburg from 882 onwards, and that a third version was put together at Altaich, “as it seems”, in 897 and carried on by two short continuations to 901. How soon after each year its entry was written is not stated in the part read; for 896 Kurze notes that news of the eastern wars seems to have reached Bavaria only that year.
sources.edition_used: Kurze 1891, in the Internet Archive scan of the University of Toronto copy

checked.read_in: Latin original, in the machine-read text of the Internet Archive scan. The letter recognition makes small slips, so Latin is quoted only where it reads cleanly. English renderings on this map are Claude's own and have not been compared with a published translation.

sources.reference: Continuation of Regino's chronicle for the years 907–967 (Continuatio Reginonis), attributed to Adalbert, later archbishop of Magdeburg. Latin edition: F. Kurze (ed.), Reginonis abbatis Prumiensis Chronicon cum continuatione Treverensi, Scriptores rerum Germanicarum in usum scholarum (Hanover, 1890), pp. 154–179.
sources.distance_note: Not established from the part read. Kurze's preface says the continuation runs from 907 to the end of 967, was written by a monk of St Maximin at Trier, and that its author is now generally held to be Adalbert, who died in 981. Kurze's margins mark the early entries (907–934) as taken from older annals, the Annales Augienses and Annales Laubacenses.

sources.derives_from_note: Printed in the same volume as Regino's chronicle (regino-chronicon), but a separate text by a later writer.

sources.reference: Widukind of Corvey, Res gestae Saxonicae (Deeds of the Saxons). Latin edition: G. Waitz (ed.), Widukindi rerum gestarum Saxonicarum libri tres, third edition, Scriptores rerum Germanicarum in usum scholarum (Hanover, 1882). Book I.17–20 is on pp. 16–18, I.38–39 on pp. 31–33, and III.44–49 on pp. 71–75.
sources.distance_note: Waitz's preface calls Widukind a Saxon and a monk of Corvey, received under Abbot Folcmar (917–942), and places the writing after the death of Archbishop Bruno (October 965), while Otto and his son were in Italy. For 955 that is about ten years after the events. For 933 it is over thirty years: Waitz says that in Henry's early years Widukind was not yet born or a small child and could draw only on tradition.
sources.edition_used: Waitz 1882 (third edition), in the Internet Archive scan of the University of Toronto copy
sources.derives_from_note: The same work as widukind-res-gestae, which is Wood's English translation of two sections. This record is the Latin text.

sources.reference: Anonymus (the anonymous notary of King Béla), Gesta Hungarorum (Deeds of the Hungarians). English translation with an introduction: Martyn Rady, “The Gesta Hungarorum of Anonymus, the Anonymous Notary of King Béla: A Translation”, author's copy in UCL Discovery (eprint 18975), 71 pages. Its acknowledgements mention the Slavonic and East European Review; the volume and page numbers of the printed version have not been checked. Rady follows the Latin edition of E. Jakubovich and D. Pais in Scriptores Rerum Hungaricarum, vol. 1 (Budapest, 1937).
sources.distance_note: Rady's introduction says the work “was most probably composed in the early years of the thirteenth century” and survives in a single copy of the late thirteenth century. It tells of the late ninth century, about three hundred years earlier. The end year 1220 here is Claude's reading of “early years”, not a date Rady gives.
sources.edition_used: Rady's English translation and introduction, in the PDF deposited at University College London. Page numbers are those printed in that PDF.

checked.read_in: English translation and Rady's introduction. The Latin was not opened, apart from the words Rady gives in brackets.
